category: Signal Processing Toolbox > Spectral Analysis & Measurements
description: Power spectral density estimation, time-frequency analysis, correlation, resampling, waveform generation, windowing and signal measurement functions from Signal Processing Toolbox.

tools.name: pwelch
tools.description: Estimate the power spectral density with Welch's method of averaged, overlapping, windowed periodograms. Averaging trades frequency resolution for a large reduction in estimate variance, which makes it the default choice for noisy real-world data. With no output arguments it plots the PSD in dB/Hz.
tools.usage:
[pxx, f] = pwelch(x, window, noverlap, nfft, fs)
[pxx, f] = pwelch(x, window, noverlap, f, fs)
pwelch(x, ___)

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: Window vector, or a scalar segment length (Hamming used), or [] for 8 segments with 50% overlap.

parameters.name: noverlap
parameters.description: Number of overlapping samples between segments; [] means 50%.

parameters.name: nfft
parameters.description: FFT length; zero-padding interpolates the spectrum but does not add resolution.

tools.notes: Longer windows give finer frequency resolution but fewer averages. Use 'power' as the final argument to get a power spectrum instead of a density.

tools.name: periodogram
tools.description: Compute the periodogram power spectral density estimate, which is a single windowed FFT magnitude squared. It has the finest possible frequency resolution for the available data but a variance that does not decrease with record length. Use it for deterministic or short signals, and pwelch for noisy ones.
tools.usage:
[pxx, f] = periodogram(x, window, nfft, fs)
[pxx, f] = periodogram(x, window, f, fs)
periodogram(x, ___)

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: Window of the same length as x; rectwin by default.

parameters.name: 'power'
parameters.description: Return a power spectrum instead of a power spectral density.

tools.name: pmtm
tools.description: Thomson multitaper power spectral density estimate. It averages periodograms computed with several orthogonal discrete prolate spheroidal (Slepian) tapers, which reduces variance without the resolution loss of segmenting. Use it for short records where you cannot afford Welch averaging.
tools.usage:
[pxx, f] = pmtm(x, nw, nfft, fs)
[pxx, pxxc, f] = pmtm(___, 'ConfidenceLevel', p)

parameters.name: 'ConfidenceLevel'
parameters.description: Probability for the returned confidence interval, e.g. 0.95.

tools.name: pburg
tools.description: Parametric PSD estimate using the Burg autoregressive method, which fits an AR model by minimizing forward and backward prediction errors. It produces smooth, high-resolution spectra from short records and always yields a stable model. Choosing the model order is the critical decision: too low smears peaks, too high creates spurious ones.
tools.usage:
[pxx, f] = pburg(x, order, nfft, fs)
[pxx, f] = pburg(x, order, nfft, fs, 'onesided')
tools.notes: arburg returns the AR coefficients themselves. pyulear and pcov are alternative AR estimators.

tools.name: pyulear
tools.description: Parametric PSD estimate from an autoregressive model fitted by the Yule-Walker (autocorrelation) method. It is fast and always stable, though slightly more biased than Burg for short records. Use it when you want a smooth parametric spectrum and have a reasonable amount of data.
tools.usage: [pxx, f] = pyulear(x, order, nfft, fs)

tools.name: cpsd
tools.description: Estimate the cross power spectral density between two signals using Welch's averaged periodogram method. The magnitude shows shared power at each frequency and the phase gives the frequency-dependent delay between the signals. It is the building block for transfer-function and coherence estimation.
tools.usage: [pxy, f] = cpsd(x, y, window, noverlap, nfft, fs)

parameters.name: x, y
parameters.description: Input signals of the same length.

tools.name: mscohere
tools.description: Estimate the magnitude-squared coherence between two signals, a normalized quantity between 0 and 1 telling you how linearly related they are at each frequency. Values near 1 indicate a consistent linear relationship; low values indicate noise or nonlinearity. Requires averaging over multiple segments to be meaningful.
tools.usage: [cxy, f] = mscohere(x, y, window, noverlap, nfft, fs)

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: Window vector or segment length; more segments give a less biased estimate.

tools.notes: With a single segment the coherence is identically 1 at every frequency, which is meaningless. Always average over several segments.

tools.name: tfestimate
tools.description: Estimate the frequency-response (transfer) function between an input and an output signal as the ratio of the cross spectrum to the input auto spectrum. This is the standard non-parametric system identification measurement for vibration, acoustics and control. Interpret the result together with mscohere to know which frequencies to trust.
tools.usage: [txy, f] = tfestimate(x, y, window, noverlap, nfft, fs)

tools.name: spectrogram
tools.description: Compute the short-time Fourier transform and display it as a time-frequency spectrogram. You control the window, overlap and FFT length, which together set the time/frequency resolution trade-off. Use it to analyse signals whose spectral content changes over time, such as speech, chirps or machine run-ups.
tools.usage:
[s, f, t] = spectrogram(x, window, noverlap, nfft, fs)
[s, f, t, ps] = spectrogram(___)
spectrogram(x, ___, 'yaxis')

parameters.name: window
parameters.description: Window vector or scalar segment length (Hamming by default).

parameters.name: noverlap
parameters.description: Number of overlapping samples; larger gives smoother time resolution.

parameters.name: 'yaxis'
parameters.description: Put frequency on the y-axis in the plot.

tools.notes: s is complex; use abs(s).^2 or the ps output for power. pspectrum(x, fs, 'spectrogram') gives an easier automatic alternative.

tools.name: stft
tools.description: Compute the short-time Fourier transform with a modern, invertible parameterization (window, OverlapLength, FFTLength, FrequencyRange). Unlike spectrogram it is designed to pair exactly with istft for perfect reconstruction. Use it for time-frequency processing where you intend to modify the STFT and transform back.
tools.usage:
s = stft(x, fs)
[s, f, t] = stft(x, fs, 'Window', win, 'OverlapLength', nov, 'FFTLength', nfft)

parameters.name: 'Window'
parameters.description: Analysis window vector; hann(128,'periodic') by default.

tools.notes: Use a periodic window and an overlap satisfying the COLA condition if you plan to invert with istft.

tools.name: istft
tools.description: Reconstruct a time-domain signal from its short-time Fourier transform by weighted overlap-add. Given the same window and overlap used by stft it recovers the original signal to within numerical precision. Use it to complete an analyse-modify-synthesize workflow such as spectral denoising or time-frequency masking.
tools.usage:
x = istft(s, fs)
[x, t] = istft(s, fs, 'Window', win, 'OverlapLength', nov, 'FFTLength', nfft, 'ConjugateSymmetric', true)

parameters.name: 'ConjugateSymmetric'
parameters.description: Set true to force a real-valued output signal.

tools.name: pspectrum
tools.description: Unified spectral analysis entry point that produces a power spectrum, spectrogram or persistence spectrum with automatic parameter selection driven by a single FrequencyResolution setting. It accepts vectors, timetables and multichannel data. Use it when you want a good answer quickly without tuning windows and overlaps.
tools.usage:
p = pspectrum(x, fs)
[p, f, t] = pspectrum(x, fs, 'spectrogram')
pspectrum(x, fs, type, Name, Value)

parameters.name: 'Leakage'
parameters.description: 0 to 1; controls the Kaiser window sidelobe trade-off.

parameters.name: 'OverlapPercent'
parameters.description: Segment overlap percentage for spectrogram mode.

tools.name: hilbert
tools.description: Compute the discrete-time analytic signal by suppressing negative-frequency components via the FFT. The imaginary part is the Hilbert transform of the input, so abs() gives the instantaneous amplitude envelope and angle() gives the instantaneous phase. Use it for envelope detection, single-sideband modulation and instantaneous frequency estimation.
tools.usage:
y = hilbert(x)
y = hilbert(x, n)

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Real input signal; matrices are processed column-wise.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: FFT length to use (input is truncated or zero-padded).

tools.notes: Edge effects are significant; discard the first and last few percent of the result. The signal should be narrowband for the envelope to be physically meaningful.

tools.name: envelope
tools.description: Compute upper and lower signal envelopes using the analytic signal, a moving RMS/peak window, or a spline fit through local extrema. It wraps the common envelope-extraction recipes in one function with a method argument. Called with no outputs it plots the signal with its envelopes overlaid.
tools.usage:
[yupper, ylower] = envelope(x)
[yupper, ylower] = envelope(x, fl, 'analytic')
[yupper, ylower] = envelope(x, np, 'peak')
[yupper, ylower] = envelope(x, wl, 'rms')

parameters.name: fl
parameters.description: Length of the FIR Hilbert filter for the 'analytic' method.

parameters.name: np
parameters.description: Peak separation in samples for the 'peak' (spline) method.

tools.name: findpeaks
tools.description: Locate local maxima in a signal and return their heights, locations, widths and prominences. The filtering options (MinPeakProminence, MinPeakDistance, MinPeakHeight, Threshold) let you reject noise peaks robustly. Prominence is usually the most reliable criterion because it is insensitive to the overall signal level.
tools.usage:
[pks, locs] = findpeaks(y)
[pks, locs, w, p] = findpeaks(y, x)
[___] = findpeaks(y, fs, Name, Value)
findpeaks(y, ___)

parameters.name: 'MinPeakProminence'
parameters.description: Minimum height a peak must stand above the surrounding baseline.

parameters.name: 'NPeaks' / 'SortStr'
parameters.description: Limit the count and order results by height.

tools.notes: To find minima call findpeaks(-y). Peaks at the very first or last sample are never reported.

tools.name: findchangepts
tools.description: Find abrupt changes in a signal's mean, variance, or linear trend by minimizing a residual-error cost with a change penalty. You can either ask for a fixed number of change points or supply a penalty that determines the number automatically. Use it to segment a recording into regimes before doing per-segment analysis.
tools.usage:
ipt = findchangepts(x)
ipt = findchangepts(x, 'MaxNumChanges', k)
ipt = findchangepts(x, 'Statistic', stat, 'MinThreshold', pen)
findchangepts(x, ___)

parameters.name: 'MaxNumChanges'
parameters.description: Maximum number of change points to return.

parameters.name: 'MinThreshold'
parameters.description: Penalty per change point; larger gives fewer changes.

parameters.name: 'MinDistance'
parameters.description: Minimum number of samples between change points.

tools.name: xcorr
tools.description: Compute the cross-correlation sequence of two signals (or the autocorrelation of one) over positive and negative lags. The lag of the peak gives the delay between the signals, which is the standard way to align two recordings. Scaling options normalize by lag count or to unit correlation at zero lag.
tools.usage:
r = xcorr(x, y)
[r, lags] = xcorr(x, y, maxlag)
[r, lags] = xcorr(x, y, maxlag, scaleopt)
[r, lags] = xcorr(x)
tools.notes: For a matrix input, xcorr returns all pairwise cross-correlations column-wise. finddelay wraps the peak-finding step.

tools.name: xcov
tools.description: Compute the cross-covariance of two signals, which is the cross-correlation after subtracting the mean from each input. Removing the DC component prevents a large common offset from dominating the correlation. Use it instead of xcorr whenever the signals have nonzero means.
tools.usage:
c = xcov(x, y)
[c, lags] = xcov(x, y, maxlag, scaleopt)

tools.name: finddelay
tools.description: Estimate the integer sample delay between two signals from the peak of their normalized cross-correlation. It returns a signed delay: positive means y lags x. Use it to synchronize multichannel recordings before further processing.
tools.usage:
d = finddelay(x, y)
d = finddelay(x, y, maxlag)

parameters.name: x, y
parameters.description: Signals to compare; can be matrices for channel-wise delays.

tools.name: resample
tools.description: Change the sample rate of a signal by a rational factor p/q using a polyphase anti-aliasing FIR filter. It also accepts non-uniformly sampled data with a time vector and resamples it onto a uniform grid. This is the general-purpose rate conversion function.
tools.usage:
y = resample(x, p, q)
[y, b] = resample(x, p, q, n, beta)
[y, ty] = resample(x, tx, fs)
y = resample(x, tx, fs, method)

parameters.name: p, q
parameters.description: Integer up- and down-sampling factors; the new rate is fs*p/q.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Half-length of the FIR filter (default 10); larger is sharper but slower.

parameters.name: tx, fs
parameters.description: Nonuniform sample times and the desired uniform output rate.

tools.notes: Endpoint transients are unavoidable; pad the signal or discard a few samples at each end. Reduce p/q with a common factor first for speed.

tools.name: decimate
tools.description: Reduce the sample rate by an integer factor after applying a lowpass anti-aliasing filter. By default it uses an order-8 Chebyshev Type I IIR filter applied with filtfilt for zero phase; an FIR option is also available. Use it for straightforward integer downsampling of already band-limited data.
tools.usage:
y = decimate(x, r)
y = decimate(x, r, n)
y = decimate(x, r, 'fir')
y = decimate(x, r, n, 'fir')

parameters.name: r
parameters.description: Integer decimation factor; keep r <= 13 per call for IIR stability.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Filter order (default 8 for IIR, 30 for FIR).

parameters.name: 'fir'
parameters.description: Use an FIR filter designed with fir1 instead of the Chebyshev IIR.

tools.notes: For r greater than 13 decimate in stages, e.g. decimate(decimate(x,5),5).

tools.name: interp
tools.description: Increase the sample rate by an integer factor using a lowpass interpolation FIR filter, so the interpolated signal matches the original at the original sample points. It is the natural counterpart to decimate for pure upsampling. The filter length and cutoff can be tuned via the l and alpha arguments.
tools.usage:
y = interp(x, r)
[y, b] = interp(x, r, l, alpha)

parameters.name: l
parameters.description: Filter length parameter (default 4); the filter has 2*l*r+1 taps.

parameters.name: alpha
parameters.description: Normalized bandwidth of the input signal (default 0.5).

tools.name: upfirdn
tools.description: Upsample, FIR filter and downsample in a single efficient polyphase operation. It gives you complete control over the interpolation filter, which resample hides. Use it for custom rate conversion, pulse shaping in communications, and multirate filter banks.
tools.usage:
y = upfirdn(x, h)
y = upfirdn(x, h, p)
y = upfirdn(x, h, p, q)

parameters.name: h
parameters.description: FIR filter impulse response applied at the upsampled rate.

tools.notes: Output length is ceil(((length(x)-1)*p + length(h))/q). Account for the filter group delay when aligning with the input.

tools.name: upsample
tools.description: Insert n-1 zeros between every sample, increasing the sample rate by n without any filtering. The result contains spectral images that must be removed by a subsequent lowpass filter. Use it as the first stage of a manually constructed interpolator.
tools.usage:
y = upsample(x, n)
y = upsample(x, n, phase)

parameters.name: phase
parameters.description: Offset of the original samples within each block, 0 to n-1.

tools.name: downsample
tools.description: Keep every nth sample and discard the rest, with no anti-alias filtering. Because it does not filter, any energy above the new Nyquist rate folds back as aliasing. Use it only on signals you have already band-limited, otherwise use decimate or resample.
tools.usage:
y = downsample(x, n)
y = downsample(x, n, phase)

parameters.name: phase
parameters.description: Which sample of each block to keep, 0 to n-1.

tools.name: chirp
tools.description: Generate a swept-frequency cosine whose instantaneous frequency varies linearly, quadratically or logarithmically with time. Chirps are the standard test signal for measuring frequency responses and for demonstrating time-frequency analysis. The initial phase can be set to build coherent multi-chirp waveforms.
tools.usage:
y = chirp(t, f0, t1, f1)
y = chirp(t, f0, t1, f1, method)
y = chirp(t, f0, t1, f1, method, phi)

parameters.name: t1, f1
parameters.description: Reference time and the instantaneous frequency at that time.

tools.notes: For the logarithmic method both f0 and f1 must be nonzero and have the same sign.

tools.name: square
tools.description: Generate a square wave with a specified duty cycle, with values of +1 and -1. It has the same calling convention as sin, taking an angle vector rather than a time and frequency. Use it for PWM, switching and digital-clock test signals.
tools.usage:
x = square(t)
x = square(t, duty)

parameters.name: duty
parameters.description: Percentage of the period at the +1 level (default 50).

tools.name: sawtooth
tools.description: Generate a sawtooth or triangle wave with values between -1 and +1. The width parameter sets where the peak occurs within each period, so width = 0.5 produces a symmetric triangle wave. Useful for sweep generators, ramp tests and audio synthesis examples.
tools.usage:
x = sawtooth(t)
x = sawtooth(t, width)

parameters.name: width
parameters.description: Fraction of the period at which the peak occurs, 0 to 1 (default 1).

tools.name: pulstran
tools.description: Generate a pulse train by repeating a prototype pulse at specified delays with optional per-pulse amplitude scaling. The prototype can be a named function (rectpuls, gauspuls, tripuls) or your own sampled waveform. Use it to build radar, ultrasound and impulse-response test signals.
tools.usage:
y = pulstran(t, d, func)
y = pulstran(t, d, func, ...)
y = pulstran(t, d, p, fs)

parameters.name: d
parameters.description: Vector of delays, or two-column matrix [delay amplitude].

parameters.name: func
parameters.description: Name of a pulse-generating function such as 'rectpuls' or 'gauspuls'.

parameters.name: p, fs
parameters.description: A sampled prototype pulse and its sample rate.

tools.name: gauspuls
tools.description: Generate a Gaussian-modulated sinusoidal RF pulse with a specified centre frequency and fractional bandwidth. It can also return the quadrature and envelope components, and compute the cutoff time for a given amplitude. Standard test signal in ultrasound and radar simulations.
tools.usage:
yi = gauspuls(t, fc, bw)
[yi, yq, ye] = gauspuls(t, fc, bw, bwr)
tc = gauspuls('cutoff', fc, bw, bwr, tpe)

parameters.name: bwr
parameters.description: Reference level in dB at which bw is measured (default -6).

parameters.name: tpe
parameters.description: Trailing pulse envelope level in dB for the 'cutoff' form.

tools.name: hann
tools.description: Return a Hann (raised-cosine) window of a given length. Its -31 dB first sidelobe and fast -18 dB/octave rolloff make it the workhorse window for general spectral analysis. Use the 'periodic' option for FFT-based analysis and filter banks, and 'symmetric' for filter design.
tools.usage:
w = hann(L)
w = hann(L, sflag)

tools.name: hamming
tools.description: Return a Hamming window, a raised cosine with nonzero endpoints tuned to cancel the first sidelobe. It gives about -43 dB sidelobes but a slower far-field rolloff than Hann. It is the default window for fir1 and for spectrogram.
tools.usage:
w = hamming(L)
w = hamming(L, sflag)
tools.example:
b = fir1(64, 0.4, hamming(65));
wvtool(hamming(64), hann(64))

tools.name: kaiser
tools.description: Return a Kaiser (Kaiser-Bessel) window whose sidelobe level is controlled continuously by the shape parameter beta. Larger beta means lower sidelobes and a wider main lobe, so a single knob trades resolution against leakage. It is the most flexible window and is used by kaiserord-based FIR designs.
tools.usage:
w = kaiser(L)
w = kaiser(L, beta)

parameters.name: beta
parameters.description: Shape parameter (default 0.5). beta = 0 is rectangular, 5 is roughly Hamming, 8.6 gives about -90 dB sidelobes.

tools.name: blackman
tools.description: Return a Blackman window, a three-term cosine window with about -58 dB sidelobes and a wide main lobe. Use it when leakage suppression matters more than resolving closely spaced tones. blackmanharris gives an even lower sidelobe floor at further cost in resolution.
tools.usage:
w = blackman(L)
w = blackman(L, sflag)

tools.name: gausswin
tools.description: Return a Gaussian window with a specified reciprocal standard deviation alpha. It is the only window whose shape is preserved under the Fourier transform, which gives the minimum possible time-bandwidth product. Common in Gabor and short-time analysis.
tools.usage:
w = gausswin(L)
w = gausswin(L, alpha)

parameters.name: alpha
parameters.description: Reciprocal of the standard deviation (default 2.5); larger alpha means a narrower window.

tools.name: tukeywin
tools.description: Return a Tukey (tapered cosine) window that is flat in the middle with cosine tapers at both ends. The parameter r sets the fraction of the window that is tapered, interpolating between a rectangular window (r = 0) and a Hann window (r = 1). Use it to suppress edge discontinuities while keeping most of the signal unweighted.
tools.usage:
w = tukeywin(L)
w = tukeywin(L, r)

tools.name: snr
tools.description: Measure the signal-to-noise ratio in dB of a signal, either by comparing it to a supplied noise signal or by estimating the fundamental power against the residual after removing harmonics and DC. Commonly used to characterize ADCs and data converters. Called with no outputs it produces an annotated spectrum plot.
tools.usage:
r = snr(x)
r = snr(x, fs)
r = snr(x, fs, n)
r = snr(x, y)
r = snr(pxx, f, 'psd')

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Signal, assumed to be a sinusoid plus noise and harmonics.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: A separate noise-only signal to compare against.

tools.notes: Related measurements: sinad, thd, sfdr and enob.

tools.name: thd
tools.description: Measure total harmonic distortion in dB relative to the fundamental, by summing the power in a given number of harmonics. It automatically detects the fundamental from the periodogram. Use it to quantify the nonlinearity of amplifiers, converters and mechanical systems.
tools.usage:
r = thd(x)
r = thd(x, fs, n)
[r, harmpow, harmfreq] = thd(___)
thd(x, fs, n)

parameters.name: 'aliased'
parameters.description: Include harmonics that alias back into the Nyquist band.

tools.name: bandpower
tools.description: Compute the average power of a signal, optionally restricted to a frequency band. It can work from the time-domain signal directly or from a precomputed power spectral density. Use it to quantify energy in EEG bands, vibration orders or channel occupancy.
tools.usage:
p = bandpower(x)
p = bandpower(x, fs, freqrange)
p = bandpower(pxx, f, 'psd')
p = bandpower(pxx, f, freqrange, 'psd')

parameters.name: freqrange
parameters.description: Two-element vector [f1 f2] giving the band of interest.

parameters.name: pxx, f
parameters.description: A PSD estimate and its frequency vector, with the 'psd' flag.
